blocks.text: A raccoon works at night. While you are asleep, it is awake and busy. It walks softly on flat feet, the way a bear walks. Its tail has dark rings all the way down. Its face has a black mask around the eyes. The best part of a raccoon is its front paws. Each one has five long fingers. A raccoon can turn a knob. It can lift a lid. It can pull a latch open. It often dips its food into water first. The water helps its fingers feel even more. So the raccoon is not washing its dinner. It is feeling it.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Reads Its Dinner
blocks.text: Long ago, people watched raccoons dunk their food in a stream and decided the raccoons were washing it. They were so sure that they wrote it into the animal's name. Its scientific name is Procyon lotor, and lotor is the Latin word for washer. In Germany a raccoon is a Waschbär, which means wash bear. In Japan it is an araiguma, which means washing bear. Half the world agrees, and half the world is wrong. Raccoons are not cleaning anything. The answer is in their paws. A raccoon's front paws are packed with tiny nerves that sense touch, and a huge part of its brain does nothing but listen to those paws. When the paws get wet, the tough skin on them softens, and the nerves feel even more than before. So a raccoon in a stream is not scrubbing its dinner. It is reading it. It runs its fingers over every bump and edge to learn what it has caught. Here is the clue that proves it. Raccoons in cages dunk their food far more often than wild raccoons do. A wild raccoon does not need to. It already spends the night with its paws under cold water, feeling for a crayfish beneath a rock it cannot see.

blocks.prompt: Everyone Is Wrong About the Raccoon
blocks.text: Watch a raccoon at the edge of a stream and it looks like it is doing the dishes. It holds a piece of food in both front paws, turns it over, rolls it, dips it under, and turns it again. People have watched this for hundreds of years and drawn the same conclusion. The raccoon is washing its dinner. They were so certain that they wrote it into the animal's name. Its scientific name is Procyon lotor, and lotor is Latin for washer. Germans call the raccoon a Waschbär, a wash bear. In Japan it is an araiguma, a washing bear. Three languages, one shared mistake. The secret is in the paws. A raccoon's front paw has five thin fingers with no webbing and no thumb, and those fingers are crowded with nerve endings that sense touch. A very large share of the raccoon's brain is set aside for nothing but the signals arriving from its paws. Your brain spends most of its attention on what your eyes send it. A raccoon's brain spends most of its attention on what its hands send it. Water makes those hands better. The tough outer layer of skin on a raccoon's paw softens when it gets wet, and softer skin feels far more detail. Dipping food is not cleaning it. It is switching on the raccoon's best sense. There is a clue that gives the whole thing away. Raccoons in cages dunk their food constantly, far more than wild raccoons do. A wild raccoon does not need to. It spends its nights with its paws already underwater, reaching under rocks and into mud for crayfish and frogs it will never see. It hunts by feel in the dark. The dunking we find so charming is the same animal doing the same thing, with nothing left to catch.

blocks.prompt: A Raccoon in a Forest Has a Hard Life
blocks.text: A raccoon in a forest has a hard life. A raccoon in a city has a career. Raccoons are native to North America, where they evolved along wooded riverbanks, hunting by touch in shallow water. Almost everything that made them good at that has turned out to make them extraordinary at living beside us. They climb, so fences and roofs are only stairs. They are nocturnal, so they work while the streets are empty. They eat nearly anything. And they have hands: five slender fingers on each front paw, wired to a brain that gives an enormous share of its sensory attention to touch alone. The result is that urban raccoons now live at population densities the woods could never support, and they get sharper about us as they go. Suzanne MacDonald, a psychologist at York University in Toronto, has spent years comparing city raccoons with country ones. The city animals are bolder, more persistent, and better at defeating the containers we invent. In 2016 Toronto rolled out a green waste bin engineered specifically to stop raccoons, at a cost of about thirty-one million dollars. It worked, mostly. Then some raccoons worked it out. None of this is new. In 1907 a researcher named H. B. Davis tested raccoons on thirteen complicated locks fitted with bolts, hooks and latches. They opened eleven of them, and when he came back a year later, they still remembered how. More recently, researchers handed raccoons a classic puzzle borrowed from an old fable: drop stones into a tube of water to float a treat up within reach. Some raccoons solved it as intended. Others tipped the whole tube over. That is not the answer the test wanted, and it is a better answer than the test expected. Winter is the one thing that reliably beats them. Raccoons do not truly hibernate. They fatten through fall, den up in a hollow tree or somebody's attic, and sleep through the worst weeks in a shallow torpor, their body temperature barely dropping. By spring, some have lost half their weight. We tend to describe all of this in a particular way. We call raccoons bandits, burglars, masked thieves. It is a flattering story, because it lets us pretend a trash can is a bank vault and that losing to a raccoon is losing to a criminal mastermind. The truth is plainer and stranger. The raccoon is not stealing from you. It has simply worked out that the richest, most reliable riverbank in North America is the one we built.

blocks.prompt: Everyone Named the Raccoon After Something It Does Not Do
blocks.text: For centuries, people watched raccoons hold food in a stream, turn it over and over in their front paws, and reached the obvious conclusion. The animal was washing its dinner. The idea stuck so hard that it is now written into three languages. The raccoon's scientific name, Procyon lotor, ends in the Latin word for washer. Germans call it the Waschbär, the wash bear. In Japan it is the araiguma, the washing bear. Three cultures, three languages, one shared mistake. The raccoon is not washing anything. To understand what it is doing, you have to look at its hands, and then at its brain. A raccoon's front paw carries five slim, mobile digits with no webbing and no opposable thumb. What it does have is nerves, in an extraordinary density. That paw is one of the finest touch organs in the animal kingdom, and the raccoon's brain is built around the fact: an enormous share of its sensory cortex, the region that processes what the body feels, is handed over to signals arriving from the front paws alone. Compare that to your own brain, which spends most of its sensory budget on vision. A raccoon does not investigate the world primarily by looking at it. It investigates by touching it. Water is the key. The tough outer layer of skin on a raccoon's paw softens when it gets wet, and softened skin transmits touch far more precisely. Dunking an object is not hygiene. It is turning up the resolution. The raccoon in the stream is not scrubbing its food, it is reading it, running its fingertips over every ridge and seam the way you might read a word in the dark. The behavior gives itself away in captivity. Caged raccoons dunk constantly, far more than wild ones do, because a wild raccoon already spends much of the night with its paws in cold water, feeling under rocks for crayfish it will never see. Those same hands make raccoons a problem. In 1907 a psychologist named H. B. Davis set raccoons in front of thirteen complicated locks involving bolts, hooks, latches and levers. They opened eleven, and when he tested them again a year later, they still remembered how. Modern researchers keep confirming the picture. Given a puzzle designed for crows, in which stones must be dropped into a tube to raise a floating treat within reach, some raccoons solved it and others simply knocked the tube over, which is not the intended answer but is arguably a better one. Cities suit them. Urban raccoons live at densities their forest cousins never reach, and studies comparing the two find the city animals harder to outwit. In 2016 Toronto spent roughly thirty-one million dollars on a green bin engineered specifically to defeat raccoons. Some raccoons defeated it anyway. And they travel. Raccoons are native to North America and nowhere else, but a handful were released at a German lake in 1934, and millions now range across Europe. In Japan the culprit was a cartoon. A 1977 television series about a boy and his pet raccoon set off an import craze, families discovered that an adorable cub becomes a powerful and destructive adult, and the ones they released established themselves across most of the country. Which returns us to those observers at the stream. They watched the animal closely and still saw the wrong thing, because they assumed it was doing a version of what a person does. It was not. It was doing something we have no equivalent for at all.
